problems.description: 26 naming violations per static analysis (convention score 0.74): module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in presence.py, rate_limit.py, registry.py, store.py; class/function casing in app.py and __init__.py. Visible registry.py/server.py are clean, so violations concentrate in the unshown modules.

ClientRegistry uses threading.Lock inside an asyncio server; the rationale is documented and defensible for cross-thread access, but asyncio.Lock would be more idiomatic if the registry stays on the event-loop thread.
broadcast() awaits each client send sequentially — delivery is serialized per client and will lag at high fan-out (the very 100-notifs/sec scenario in the story's review turn).
No test files appear in the diff for this session; store, rate_limit, and presence logic ship unverified.

strengths: Clean modular decomposition: server.py (transport/routing), registry.py (client tracking), plus store/rate_limit/presence/app as separate single-responsibility modules.
Modern typed Python throughout: type hints, from __future__ import annotations, PEP 604 unions, concise docstrings.
Thoughtful thread-safety decision in ClientRegistry with the lock choice explicitly documented.
Consistent error handling in message routing (invalid JSON, unknown type, missing fields, target-not-found) with uniform system error messages.
Health endpoint served on the same port via the process_request hook — pragmatic, avoids a second HTTP server.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-architected greenfield Session 1 — sound modular WebSocket design with clean typed Python and good error handling (architectural fit 0.85), undercut only by a cluster of naming-convention violations driving the mechanical convention score to 0.74.

problems.description: Broadcast routing is keyed off a payload field ('channel'): any broadcast whose payload happens to carry a 'channel' key is silently narrowed to that channel's subscribers instead of reaching everyone. This is a subtle semantic coupling between data and routing metadata; a dedicated envelope field would be less surprising.
Subscription counts are unbounded: a client can create an arbitrary number of channels with no cap, which could grow the registry's _subscriptions map indefinitely (no max channels per client).
remove() walks all channels (O(#channels)) on every disconnect to prune subscriptions; correct but linear per teardown — negligible at current scale, worth noting if the fan-out grows.

Measured convention score of 0.74 is driven by pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, __init__.py, presence.py, rate_limit.py, store.py); the only touched file listed (registry.py: module-level constants UPPER_CASE) introduces no new constants in this diff. The commit's own additions are convention-clean — see summary.

strengths: Leak-free subscription bookkeeping: remove() prunes a disconnecting client's subscriptions and deletes emptied channels, matching the same hygiene already applied in unsubscribe().
Consistent thread-safety: all map/set mutations stay under the existing _lock, using setdefault/discard idioms that mirror the established registry style.
connections_for_channel() guards with 'if cid in self._clients', avoiding KeyError on stale subscriptions between remove and broadcast.
Good HTTP hygiene: urlsplit to strip query strings, unquote on channel names, and a shared _json_response helper that deduplicates the previous /health response body.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-factored feature addition that cleanly extends the existing dispatch/registry/HTTP patterns with proper cleanup, locking, and tests — the 0.74 measured convention score is inflated by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touches, so I rate its own additions higher.

problems.description: Dual-state tracking: local ClientRegistry and the new global RedisPresence both model client state, creating two sources of truth that can drift (local sockets vs Redis presence) without a clear reconciliation path.

26 measured convention violations across the expanded modules — app.py/__init__.py have PascalCase class issues and __init__.py has snake_case function issues; module-level constants in presence.py, store.py, registry.py, and rate_limit.py are not UPPER_CASE.

presence/store/redis are initialized to None with no explicit fail-fast or graceful-degradation contract when Redis or SQLite is unavailable; behavior may silently change (e.g., routing falls back without logging).

strengths: Clean single-responsibility module split: presence.py (state), store.py (history), server.py (routing/transport).
Redis set-based presence is O(1) for membership/counts, survives restarts, and the docstring clearly scopes process-local vs global state.
Consistent typing and async conventions, idempotent teardown in remove_client (unsubscribes before deleting keys), and env-config with sensible defaults.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured multi-instance integration commit (Redis bus + SQLite history) with a clear module split, slightly weighed down by measured naming violations and a dual-state (local registry + global presence) maintenance risk.

problems.description: Speculative transport abstraction: BaseTransport interface is introduced with only one shipped implementation (WebSocket), despite the docstring advertising SSE/polling/raw TCP. This is YAGNI debt until a second transport actually lands, and adds ~200 net lines of indirection.

26 convention violations (score 0.74) include module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in the new transport/__init__.py, presence.py, registry.py, and store.py, plus class/function naming issues in app.py and __init__.py — several appear in newly-added files, not just pre-existing code.

+19 imports across 6 new files raises the import surface; worth a pass for unused imports since the server.py diff removes the websockets imports cleanly, but the transport package may carry redundant ones.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: routing/registry/presence/persistence logic now deals only with opaque connection objects, decoupling the core from the websockets wire protocol.

Backward-compatible seam: transport is injectable via constructor parameter with env-var default, preserving the existing NotificationServer API for existing callers and enabling fake-transport tests.
Removes websockets imports from the core module, shrinking its dependency surface (ServerConnection, Request, Response, Headers, ConnectionClosed all moved out).
Preserves the existing registry/presence/store patterns untouched rather than rewriting them.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-shaped dependency-inversion refactor that decouples the notification core from the websockets protocol, slightly held back by a speculative single-implementation transport abstraction and 26 low-severity naming/convention violations (0.74).

problems.description: Measured convention score 0.74 with 26 violations across the 8 touched files: module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in rate_limit.py/presence.py/registry.py/store.py, a non-PascalCase class in app.py, and snake_case/constant naming issues in __init__.py.

_parse_since normalizes timestamps to the same UTC-offset ISO format as now_iso() so SQL filters by string comparison; chronologically correct only while both formats stay in lockstep, so format drift would silently break history filtering.

Fixed-window Redis INCR limiter allows a burst of up to limit messages at a window boundary (100/min default); acceptable for the use case but a sliding-window or token bucket would be smoother at higher limits.

strengths: Rate limiting lives in shared Redis, so the limit is enforced consistently across every server instance — the same cross-instance design the existing RedisPresence and pub/sub bus already use.
Background cleanup task lifecycle (create in start(), cancel + await in close()) mirrors the existing _consume_bus task pattern exactly.
RateLimiter is small, single-purpose, and takes the injected Redis client, matching the DI style used elsewhere and keeping it testable.
New config follows the established constructor-param + env-var + DEFAULT_ constant pattern already used for host/port/db_path.
commit_reviews.summary: Cross-cutting rate limiting and message TTL retention fit the Redis/SQLite architecture and existing task/DI patterns well (architectural fit 0.85); the measured 0.74 convention score flags mostly file-level naming issues across the story codebase, while the new rate_limit.py itself reads convention-clean — a possible file-level rather than line-level attribution in the measurement.

compounding_issues: Session 2 keyed channel routing off a payload field ('channel') — any broadcast whose payload carried a 'channel' key was silently narrowed to that channel instead of reaching everyone; this data/routing-metadata coupling persisted until the Session 4 transport refactor
Session 2 introduced unbounded per-client channel subscriptions with no cap, letting the registry's _subscriptions map grow without bound (only partially addressed by Session 5 rate limiting)

Session 3 wired Redis pub/sub directly inline into server.py (+158 lines, the costliest session at $2.14 / 739s) before any transport abstraction existed, embedding integration debt that Session 4's refactor (194 lines rewritten) had to repay
Session 2's disconnect path prunes subscriptions in O(#channels) per teardown — negligible at small scale but a latent scaling cost carried forward
Session 2 expanded the feature surface (channels) without matching test coverage for the new routing semantics, leaving the payload-collision edge case untested into later sessions
key_decisions: WebSocket-first notification server with per-client unique IDs as the Session 1 greenfield foundation
Channel-based subscription model where routing metadata rides in the message payload itself (Session 2)
Redis pub/sub as the message backbone with multi-worker subscription/delivery plus a separate presence module and MessageStore persistence layer (Session 3)
Extraction of a pluggable Transport interface (transport/base.py + transport/websocket.py) in Session 4, decoupling WebSocket from SSE/polling/TCP and repaying the Session 3 integration debt
Operational hardening in Session 5 — per-client rate limiting via Redis counters, TTL-based cleanup, and paginated persistent history layered on the Session 3 store
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 stood up a flat 357-line server class, Session 2 broadened the surface with channel subscriptions (the one flat spot: new routing semantics outpaced test coverage), Session 3 was the heavy pivot — Redis pub/sub integration, presence, and persistence tripled the system's size (728→943 code lines and the largest token/cost/duration footprint at $2.14 and 739s) but did so by embedding Redis inline, incurring debt that Session 4's transport-layer refactor explicitly paid down (101 lines removed, server.py rewritten into MessageStore / BaseTransport / NotificationServer seams). Session 5 built cleanly on that settled architecture, adding rate limiting, TTL cleanup, and paginated history to reach a green 1116-line / 1195-test-line final state with all sessions exiting 0 and convention adherence stable at 0.745 throughout.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherence arc — greenfield, feature, integration, refactor, cross-cutting hardening — that improved monotonically by paying down the Session 3 integration debt with a Session 4 pluggable-transport refactor, the only real drag being Session 2's data-coupled channel routing and its under-tested edge cases.
